title: wellness and life balance for sports medicine physicians: recognizing physician burnout
display_name: Wellness and Life Balance for Sports Medicine Physicians: Recognizing Physician Burnout
abstract: the american medical association estimates the cost of physician burnout in the united states at 4.6 billion dollars annually (1). as sports medicine physicians, we have either trained in or evolved into the concept of the "triple aim," which are as follows: 1) improved patient care and satisfaction, 2) lower costs, and 3) better outcomes. late to the party is the concept of "physician satisfaction." it is past time to address wellness and burnout in medicine and sports medicine, to understand the prevalence of burnout in our profession, to develop strategies that reduce physician suicide, and to support the "joy of practice." wellness and life balance should be a "no brainer" for those trained to care for people, but it does not come naturally to hard driving professionals willing to put others above themselves at all times. the stress of physician life is real, and life balance is essential for physician success. our profession has moved away from the every other and every third night call schedules that ruled resident life during physician training in my era. good patient care demands alert minds to solve problems quickly and accurately. as with everything in life, physicians exist under a bell curve and outliers on time spent working often rise to high positions within our management systems. our local newspaper highlighted the new ceo at a major area medical system; a physician who works 22 hours per day (2). that leaves 2 hours per day for personal hygiene, sleep, and family interactions. this seems typical of medical organization ceos and medical school deans; also, it sets an expectation that the rest of us should be equally energetic and sleepless. the philosophy of "leaders leaving loudly" is difficult to endorse when leaders never leave. family, exercise, sleep, nutrition, and time away are essential to navigating demands on time and executing plans to reduce stress. it is essential for physicians to make time for family and self, within the context of a well-balanced career. think sports wellness for sports physicians athlete life is about enhancing physical performance, which requires a balance of training work load, energy stores (nutrition), sleep, and training breaks (rest) to minimize the risk of overuse injury and overtraining syndrome. an ideal training plan involves multiple progressive training load cycles with the shortest cycle at 1 wk and the longest at 1 year. there are 7 d available in each week cycle, and the "training standard" is 6 d, alternating hard and easy workouts, with one full day dedicated to rest. throughout a year-long cycle, there are periodic week- long training breaks, and a year-round athlete's schedule (with good coaching) will incorporate a full month away from training each year. translate this to wellness and life balance for a sports physician. sports physician life is about cognitive performance that hinges on a balance of work load and personal time to minimize risk of medical error and "overwork syndrome" (burnout). the concept of time away each day, week, and year is important to maintain a "normal" life. think of overtraining and burnout as similar problems. "athlete overtraining" leads to fatigue and an inability to improve performance. "physician burnout" leads to exhaustion of emotional strength or loss of motivation and inability to perform efficiently. it was recently reported that a family physician seeing patients for 28 hours per week spends an additional 7.5 hours per week completing charts and other clerical patient care duties during evenings and on weekends (3). this out of clinic time commitment takes away from the personal time required to maintain health and wellness and lends to burnout. the three-legged milk stool a three-legged stool is stable on uneven surfaces and is commonly used while milking cows by hand. as a child, our family vacationed on the farm where my mother was raised. my uncles milked by hand, and i wanted to "help." they would let me milk the gentlest cow in the herd, in part to keep me out of the way. i used a three-legged stool. then, i noticed my uncles used one-legged stools, so i wanted to use one too. after some persistent pestering, my uncle took me aside with a one-legged stool and a bucket. he had me sit on the stool and assume a milking position with the bucket between my knees. when i finally steadied myself, he gave me a gentle nudge, and i found myself sitting on the barn floor, bucket on its side. he then said, "you are not strong enough for a one-legged stool, if you spill the milk, i lose money." so i was back on a three-legged stool. a one-legged stool is like personal resilience and a risky way to approach the stresses of medical practice. physician wellness depends on a three-legged stool; a combination of system efficiency, supportive work culture, and personal resilience. without a strong effort to change system efficiency and workplace culture, physicians are left with personal resilience as the sole strategy to navigate a known stressful career path. maintaining the joy of practice, reducing burnout, and improving career satisfaction has more to do with fixing system inefficiencies (magnified by electronic health records and increasing demands for patient care volumes) and righting the course of work culture that seems to have little regard for personal time. shanafelt and noseworthy (4) have described a three-pronged approach that identifies and promotes a culture of wellness, efficiency of practice, and supporting personal resilience. a culture of wellness requires creating and supporting a work environment that promotes self-care; personal and professional growth; and compassion for colleagues, patients, and self from the top down. efficiency of practice is a rough mathematical calculation of value added using clinical work accomplished divided by the time and energy spent. improving the denominator with strategies that address the speedbumps in clinical care will often increase the numerator with an amplified return on the investment. finally, developing personal resilience with training in the individual skills, behaviors, and attitudes that contribute to personal physical, emotional, and social well-being, including the prevention of burnout. all three strategies contribute to the joy of practice for individual physicians and improve the bottom line for an organization. wellness and life balance why is joy of practice, wellness, and work-life balance important? the statistics surrounding physicians are not good for burn out, alcohol and drugs, depression, and suicide. in a 2019 publication, shanafelt et al. (5) reviewed maslach survey results for 2011, 2014, and 2017 and found an overall rate of physician burnout of 51%, with family medicine ranking third among specialties at 55%. these surveys were widely distributed, and although the return was less than 20%, the results are assumed to reflect the state of physicians as a whole. the good news is the numbers have returned to 2011 levels more or less, from the higher levels of 2014. among physicians, depression prevalence is similar to the general population, estimated at 12% for men and 19.5% for women. however, the suicide rate for physicians is 1.4 times greater for men and 2.3 times greater for women than the general population (6). the 28 to 40 per 100,000 physician "lives lost" to suicide each year, more than twice the suicide rate in the general population, is a part of the "cost of burnout" (7). our response as a profession has been "what is wrong with them?" we should have been asking "what is wrong with us?" why have we, as a profession, not responded to the issue and what can we do to reduce burnout in our colleagues? physician burnout and depression have similar symptoms; clinical tools and a high index of suspicion are needed to differentiate between the two. "erroneously labeling a physician's distress as burnout may prevent or delay appropriate treatment of [major depressive disorder] ." (8). in a survey of 7288 physicians, 12.9% of male and 21.4% of female physicians met diagnostic criteria for substance abuse disorder (sad), which is slightly higher than the general population (9,10). sad has strong ties to both depression and burnout (11). the cost of burnout includes lives lost (not all attributable to burnout), early retirements, physicians exiting the field, increases in error rates, decreases in patient satisfaction, among other detriments to the medical field and our patients. the common denominator is the loss of joy in practice. some have called the loss of joy "moral injury" reflecting a breach of expectations in the current medical climate that reaches beyond burnout (12,13). the premise behind this label suggests that burnout lays blame on physicians, and moral injury shifts the conversation to the causes of physician career dissatisfaction rooted in the insurmountable task of simultaneously satisfying patients, employers, clinics, hospitals, payers, and ourselves (and families). what drives burnout and what are the effects among physicians? burnout is driven by high workloads, workflow inefficiencies, documentation time, and loss of meaning in work fueled by unrealistic expectations of the workplace. i think back to my training and early practice years compared with current in-training and early career physicians. i was trained with paper medical records, paid on patient volume (fee for service), provided individual health care with subjective outcomes, and medical knowledge was doubling about every 7 years (14). today, we are challenged by dante's inferno of the electronic medical record mainly designed to capture billing, paid by an elusive combination of work relative value units and value of care (cost and quality), monitored electronically with "big data," expected to influence population health, and keep abreast of medical knowledge that doubles about every 3 months (14). developing a culture of wellness a culture of wellness requires creating and promoting a work environment with normative values, attitudes, and behaviors that promote self-care, personal growth, and compassion. to accomplish a cultural shift, we must define professional wellness as a priority, regularly assess physician well-being, and create intervention strategies to foster workplace support. leaders modeling well behavior strategies are critical to this effort because a 22-h work day in the leadership realm does not set reasonable expectations for those lower on the workforce organizational chart. personal resilience will always be a part of physician survival skills, but tantamount to reduced burnout and moral injury is a culture shift in the corporate suite of medical care organizations. we all need a set of individual skills, behaviors, and attitudes that contribute to our physical, emotional, and social well-being; however, the major factors that drive burnout are housed in the organization. from the organization level, there are several ways to promote personal resilience and a well workplace including providing assistance for physicians in accomplishing basic life tasks, establishing a quiet space for physicians to refresh and recharge (the old hospital physicians' lounge), providing on-site exercise facilities, offering peer support and mentoring programs, and creating off-site psychological counseling service opportunities. training for personal resilience alone is not enough and is insufficient without addressing workplace culture and system efficiency within an organization. what can you do to preserve wellness and life balance? within our "fraternity" of sports medicine physicians, we face similar issues, and we should strive to improve wellness and life balance within our ranks. develop a mentoring network to help each other, and especially our younger colleagues, navigate the systems and daily changes of the workplace. work with your practice organization to improve the workplace culture and optimize the systems for efficient practice of medicine. on an individual basis, prioritizing the important parts of your life is critical to avoiding burnout and maintaining life balance (table 1). in the scope of life, the factors that are critical to a successful career are family, fitness, fatigue mitigation (sleep), workplace support, and financial security. think of how you can plan your day, week, month, and year to preserve your life balance. it is common in medicine to see the order of life priorities reversed with family, fitness, and sleep pushed aside to advance a career (table 2). the personal and indirect cost of "business as usual" can be high for both physicians and organizations, and as many learn too late, there are no "do-overs." is business as usual worth it?table 1: prioritizing your life decisionstable 2: tips for maintaining life balance

title: an osteoid osteoma as an undiagnosed cause of three years of severe pain
display_name: An Osteoid Osteoma As an Undiagnosed Cause of Three Years of Severe Pain

authorships.name: Thomas Hartmann
institutions: Hospital of the Brothers of St. John of God

institutions: Hospital of the Brothers of St. John of God

abstract: osteoid osteoma is a benign, bone-forming tumor representing approximately 12% of all benign bone neoplasias in young individuals [1]. first described by jaffe [2] in 1935, it has a predilection for the lower extremity, with 50% or more of lesions occurring in the femur and tibia. of the remaining lesions, approximately 30% are equally distributed among the spine, hand, and foot [3]. there are different types of osteoid osteomas, each with differing degrees of associated osteosclerosis [4]. pain is the leading and, in its early stages, often the only symptom of the disease and is typically described as mild and intermittent at first, later becoming more constant, more severe, and worse at night. intense pain may be present even before the lesion is radiologically apparent. male patients are more often affected than female patients by a ratio of 2:1, and the tumor is rare in the african-american population [5]. trauma has been considered a contributing factor [6]. there are no pathognomonic signs or symptoms that unerringly lead to the correct diagnosis. patients may undergo multiple procedures for the treatment of pain and/or unnecessary surgical procedures, leading to a reduced of quality of life, as in the case we present. although there are many reports of this tumor in the surgical literature, they leave the question of pain and its treatment aside [7-9]. case report after manually lifting heavy items, a 44-yr-old man developed pain and paresthesias in the proximal phalanx of the fifth digit, with a pain level of 5-7 of 10 on the visual analog scale (vas). the finger was slightly thickened, without signs of inflammation; however, it was extremely sensitive to external pressure and active or passive motion. the pain was thought to be from neuronal compression because neither radiographs nor computerized tomography (ct) revealed morphological pathology of the bony structures. therapy with nonsteroidal analgesics was started, followed by local infiltration with anesthetics and cryotherapy. as none of these treatments resulted in pain relief, surgical neurolysis of the digital nerve was performed 4 mo after the initial trauma. intraoperatively, the tissue around the nerves appeared to be thickened and was removed. neither the proximal phalanx nor the proximal interphalangeal joint appeared to be affected. no new information was obtained from another radiograph and ct postoperatively. however, a radionuclide bone scan indicated that an inflammatory process might be present. meanwhile, the patient was suspected of overreacting to his pain and was subsequently referred for psychopharmacological drug therapy. this treatment had no effect on the pain level. by this point, the patient had stopped working and had repeatedly contacted various emergency health facilities in his community to get pain relief. on physical examination, the patient localized the pain exactly and described it as burning and sticking in nature, causing him to be unable to sleep most of the night. local anesthetic infiltration, although beneficial at first, became ineffective. pharmacological pain management included nonsteroidal drugs and opioids, as well as tricyclic antidepressants, and was reinforced by physical therapy and psychological guidance. magnetic resonance imaging (mri) revealed some swelling of the tendinous sheaths and was followed by another surgical neurolysis of the digital nerve. the diagnosis of tendinous synovitis was confirmed by macroscopic examination, as well as by inflammatory reaction in the histologic specimen. because the clinical picture indicated the presence of a complex regional pain syndrome, the patient was treated with repeated stellate ganglion blocks, followed by intravenous regional anesthesia with guanethidine to block peripheral sympathetic efferents. blockade of the sensory afferents in the brachial plexus was accomplished by using a continuous axillary catheter. these measures reduced pain to a score of 3 on the vas, but for only a limited time. multiple additional surgical interventions were subsequently performed for removal of chronically inflamed tissue or neuronal decompression. nearly 3 yr after the patient first presented with the digital pain, an endoscopic thoracic sympathectomy was performed to repeat the beneficial effect of the sympathetic blocks. the pain recurred postoperatively after 3 days with the same intensity as he had originally experienced (vas score 5-7). the patient reacted with desperation and was becoming suicidal, demanding amputation of the painful digit. at this point, another radiograph for the first time revealed a hypodense oval area in the distal portion of the basal phalanx, measuring 8 x 5 mm and surrounded by a hyperdense border, indicating osteolytic destruction of the bone. surgical removal of the destroyed bone mass followed. examination of the histologic specimen revealed the presence of an osteoid osteoma. after this operation, the patient was immediately free from pain. one year later the patient is still pain free and fully reintegrated into the workplace. discussion the radiographic hallmark of osteoid osteoma is the central nidus, a 2- to 10-mm focus of osteoid nested in a more radiolucent fibrous stroma, surrounded by marginal sclerosis. current treatment is excision of the nidus, although other treatments, such as percutaneous tomography-guided thermocoagulation, have been described [2]. several hypotheses have been proposed to explain the intensity of the pain. it was originally suggested that nerve endings might be stimulated by the high pressure because of the increased blood flow within the tumor [11]. there are also nerve fibers identified in the fibrous zone around the nidus, which are presumed to be components of the autonomic nervous system [12]. this could explain the pain reduction after sympathetic blocks in our patient. the pain in our patient was also reduced to some extent by non-steroidal antiinflammatory drugs, which suggests some contribution of prostaglandins to pain development in this tumor. prostaglandins may directly stimulate free nerve endings inside or close to the tumor by lowering the nociceptive threshold [13,14]. other diagnostic entities that may be manifested as extremity pain related or unrelated to trauma include tumors (either primary or metastatic), infectious or aseptic inflammatory processes of the bone and/or neighboring structures, and all the pathologies of regional somatosensoric and sympathetic nerve structures, or arthrotic alterations of the joints. plain radiographs do not provide a clear diagnosis of osteoid osteoma [15]. because of the prominent marginal sclerosis of osteoid osteomas, ct is more sensitive [16]. nevertheless, false-negative results have been reported [9], as illustrated by our case. it is thus far from clear what role mri might may play in diagnosis [17,18]. mri remains a less informative method when osteoid osteoma is suspected [8]. although diagnosis can almost always be made with radionuclide bone scan [19], the scan performed early in our case showed only signs of an inflammatory process retrospectively confirmed by our radiologists two years later. persistent bone pain accompanied by nonspecific radiographic as well as scintigraphic findings should make one suspicious of osteoid osteoma [3]. this suspicion should encourage more persistent efforts to reach a diagnosis and could thus help to reduce ineffective, unspecific measures widely used to treat pain. the authors thank prof. robert sladen and prof. dan sessler for their critical review of the manuscript.
